newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU agrees aid for Credit Lyonnais.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees aid for Credit Lyonnais.

text.p: The European Commission, agreeing a large shot of emergency aid for embattled French bank Credit Lyonnais, said on Wednesday a survival plan would take "considerably" more subsidies than originally believed.
In a speedy move, it gave the go ahead for 3.9-billion French francs ($765.6 million) in urgent aid pending new restructuring measures to be submitted by the French government.
European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told a news conference, however, that the new plan was unlikely to go through without "real and susbtantive" divestments.
Credit Lyonnais, once the world's largest bank outside Japan, is already benefiting from a rescue plan worth a maximum 45 billion francs which was cleared by the Commission in July last year.
Speaking in an unusually conciliatory tone, Van Miert said that plan had failed to live up to expectations due to the lacklustre French market and the bank's poor image in public opinion.
"(Credit Lyonnais') rivals said at the time that the Commission had not been tough enough and that it (the 1995 rescue plan) would turn the bank into a 'super champion'", Van Miert said,
"We see today that that was not the case."
He declined to say how much the French authorities might have to pay for another bail out, but said it would be a "considerable figure".
EU rules on rescue aid for ailing businesses allow for subsidies to be paid if they are limited to putting a company back on its feet without harming competition.

Asked whether the Commission would call for the early sale of Lyonnais in return for further help, Van Miert said it was no use pushing for the privatisation of the bank before it was made attractive again.
"If you are interested in Credit Lyonnais, I'm sure you can get it for a symbolic franc; that is with the bad assets as well," he joked.
The French government has committed itself to privatising Lyonnais by the year 2000

The emergency aid agreed on Wednesday included cancellation of the obligation put on Lyonnais in 1995 to grant a loan below market rate to a state-backed vehicle to which it transferred some 130 billion francs of shaky assets. The interest on the loan was 85 percent of what would have been the market rate.
The bank had said that it would loose three billion francs in funding the loan this year, which analysts said could drag it into a two billion franc half-year loss.

Van Miert said that provided the French government formally notified the Commission quickly of the measures in the pipeline, the EU executice could take a decision on the new plan by the end of the year.
French bank Societe Generale has challenged the Commission decision on the 1995 rescue plan before the European Court in Luxembourg. ($= 5.094 FrF)
